p: Canterbury fills up with visitors on weekends and during the summer, with coach parties, students and day trippers all heading for the same streets. That's exactly why it helps to have a booked activity like an escape game in your back pocket. Pick your slot first and plan your sightseeing around it, rather than the other way round.

If you're new to escape rooms, a little preparation helps. Have a quick chat with your group before you go in about how you'll work. Some teams split up to search, others stick together and talk everything through. Either can work, but the key is sharing what you find. Small details, like a number scratched on a frame or a colour that keeps cropping up, are often the key to the next lock.
Mixed-age groups do well here too. Grandparents often bring patience and lateral thinking, while kids bring speed and sharp eyes. Put them together and you've got a properly balanced team.

Canterbury Riverside is handy for both of the city's railway stations, with Canterbury West a short stroll away for trains towards London, and the city centre within easy walking distance. Afterwards, wander down to the Westgate Towers, the medieval gateway into the city, and the lovely Westgate Gardens beside the Stour. River tours on the Stour run in the warmer months, giving you a different view of the old buildings. St Augustine's Abbey, part of the Canterbury World Heritage Site alongside the cathedral, is worth a look for history fans, and the Marlowe Theatre puts on everything from big touring shows to panto. If you've got a car, the seaside at Whitstable is a short drive north for oysters and a stroll along the harbour.
